title: CPVC Pipe Size Guide for Indian Homes: Bathroom, Kitchen and Geyser Lines
metaTitle: CPVC Pipe Size Guide for Indian Homes: Bathrooms & Geysers
description: Understand common CPVC sizes for main, branch, bathroom, kitchen and geyser lines, plus the pressure and flow factors that determine final sizing.
bodyHtml:
Quick answer: A common residential starting point is 25 mm or 20 mm for distribution and branch lines, with 15 mm connections near individual fixtures. This is not a universal sizing rule. The correct CPVC size depends on available pressure, route length, number of fixtures, simultaneous use, fittings, pump operation and the manufacturer’s pipe data. A plumber or plumbing designer should approve the final layout before concealed work begins.

Pipe size affects how a plumbing system feels in everyday use. When a branch is too small, a shower may weaken as soon as the kitchen tap opens. When the main line is reduced too early, two bathrooms may compete for flow. Increasing every pipe size is not a complete solution either; it raises cost and may increase the volume of water that must be cleared before hot water reaches a distant fixture.

This guide gives homeowners and contractors a practical way to discuss CPVC sizing. It is a planning reference, not a substitute for hydraulic design or the latest manufacturer instructions.

Common CPVC Size Planning for Residential Lines

Line or fixtureCommon starting rangeWhat decides the final size
Main internal distribution line20–25 mm or larger where designedNumber of bathrooms, source pressure, building height and simultaneous demand
Bathroom branch serving several fixtures20 mm is a common starting pointShower type, geyser, basin, health faucet and route length
Individual basin or health-faucet connection15 mm is commonly usedFixture inlet, pressure and local plumbing practice
Shower or mixer connection15–20 mmRequired flow, rain-shower demand, mixer design and pressure balance
Kitchen sink mixer15–20 mmSink flow, purifier or appliance branches and distance from source
Geyser inlet and hot-water outlet15–20 mmGeyser connection, shower demand, route length and manufacturer guidance

 

These ranges are deliberately described as starting points. Nominal size, internal diameter, SDR and schedule are related but not identical. Two pipes with the same nominal size may not have the same internal waterway. Check the selected product data rather than relying only on the number printed in a quotation.

Six Factors That Change the Required Size

1. Available water pressure

Gravity supply from an overhead tank behaves differently from a pressure-pump system. Low source pressure cannot be corrected simply by increasing the final fixture connection. Tank height, pump setting and pressure losses across the full route must be considered.

2. Number of fixtures on one branch

A pipe feeding one basin has a lower demand than a branch serving a shower, basin, health faucet and geyser. The upstream branch should retain enough capacity before reducing near individual points.

3. Simultaneous use

Design for realistic use. In a family home, a shower, kitchen sink and another bathroom may operate together. Sizing only for one open tap can produce an uncomfortable pressure drop during peak use.

4. Route length and fittings

Long routes, small valves, filters, multiple elbows and sudden reductions add resistance. A compact flat and a multistorey house may therefore need different distribution logic even when they have the same number of fixtures.

5. Fixture flow requirement

A standard basin tap, high-flow bath spout and large rain shower do not need the same supply. Select the fixtures before freezing the concealed pipe sizes, especially in premium bathrooms.

6. Hot-water delivery time

An unnecessarily large, long hot-water line holds more water. Users may wait longer for warm water and waste the cold water standing in the route. Hot-water sizing should balance flow with route volume and insulation.

Sizing by Area

Bathroom lines

Keep the bathroom branch adequately sized until the flow divides toward the shower, basin, health faucet and geyser. Do not reduce the branch at the shaft and then expect a high-flow shower to perform well at the far end. Confirm the mixer and shower inlet requirements before plastering.

Kitchen lines

A kitchen may need connections for the sink mixer, water purifier and dishwasher. Plan separate accessible valves where needed. If the kitchen is far from the source, route length and bends may have a larger effect than the final short connection to the mixer.

Geyser lines

Match the geyser inlet and outlet connections, safety-valve arrangement and hot-water demand. Keep the hot route as direct as practical and support it properly. The hot and cold sides of a mixer should receive compatible flow so temperature adjustment remains stable.

How Prayag’s CPVC Range Fits Residential Planning

Prayag’s CPVC pipe range covers sizes from 15 mm upward across multiple SDR and schedule options. That broad availability does not mean every house needs a large pipe. It allows the system designer to select main, branch and fixture sizes according to the project rather than forcing one diameter throughout.

Use compatible fittings from the Prayag Pipes & Fittings range and check the latest catalogue for dimensions, pressure class, temperature suitability and jointing instructions.

Questions to Ask Before Approving the Plumbing Drawing

  • What is the source pressure and is a booster pump planned?
  • How many fixtures will each branch serve?
  • Which fixtures may operate at the same time?
  • What is the longest route from the source to a bathroom or kitchen?
  • How many elbows, filters, valves and reducers are on that route?
  • Will a rain shower, bath spout or other high-flow fixture be installed?
  • What nominal size, SDR or schedule has been specified?
  • Has the sizing been checked against the selected CPVC product data?

Common CPVC Sizing Mistakes

  • Using 15 mm throughout the house because it matches many fixture inlets.
  • Reducing the main or bathroom branch before the flow splits.
  • Choosing high-flow fixtures after concealed plumbing is complete.
  • Ignoring pressure loss through filters, valves and long horizontal runs.
  • Assuming a pressure pump removes the need for correct pipe sizing.
  • Mixing nominal size and actual internal diameter in calculations.

Installation and Handover Checks

  • Confirm pipe and fitting sizes against the approved drawing.
  • Use square cuts, remove burrs and follow the specified solvent-cement method.
  • Allow the required curing time before pressure testing.
  • Test the complete network before wall closure.
  • Run fixtures together during functional testing to check practical flow.
  • Save photos showing the route and size transitions.

For more context on material performance, see Why Prayag CPVC Pipes Are a Smart Plumbing Choice. Product selection should still be approved for the specific site.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is 15 mm CPVC enough for a bathroom?

It may be suitable for individual fixture connections. A branch serving several fixtures often needs a larger starting size, depending on pressure, route length and simultaneous demand.

What CPVC size is commonly used for a geyser?

Many residential installations use 15 mm or 20 mm near a geyser, but the connection size, hot-water demand, route and product guidance must decide the final selection.

Can I use 20 mm CPVC for the whole house?

Not as a universal rule. A small flat and a large independent house have different demand, distance and pressure conditions. Main and branch lines should be sized from the layout.

Does a larger CPVC pipe always improve pressure?

No. Pipe diameter affects friction loss, but source pressure, pump setting, elevation, valves and fixture restrictions also matter.

Should hot- and cold-water lines use the same size?

They may in some layouts, but not automatically. The hot route, heater connection and fixture demand should be reviewed separately.

Who should approve the final CPVC size?

A qualified plumber, plumbing consultant or project engineer should approve it using the actual layout and selected product specifications.

Explore the Right Prayag Solution

Explore Prayag CPVC pipes and compatible fittings, then share the final layout with a qualified installer. For product or dealer assistance, contact Prayag.

Final Recommendation

Use 15 mm, 20 mm and 25 mm only as common planning references, not a copy-and-paste design. Keep main and branch capacity until the flow divides, match high-flow fixtures early, and check route losses and source pressure. The correct CPVC size is the smallest properly engineered size that delivers the required flow without unnecessary pressure loss or hot-water delay.
